questions.q: What makes a base class 'abstract' in C++?
options: It has no data members
It contains at least one pure virtual function (declared with = 0)
It is declared with the keyword abstract
It has a private constructor
questions.explain: A class becomes abstract — unable to be instantiated directly — once it declares at least one pure virtual function.

questions.q: Why does the override keyword matter when defining a derived class's version of a virtual function?
options: It makes the function run faster
It is required for the function to compile at all
It makes the function private automatically
It tells the compiler to verify the function actually matches a virtual function in the base, catching signature mismatches
questions.explain: override is a compiler-checked safeguard: if the signature doesn't match any virtual function in the base class, the code fails to compile instead of silently creating an unrelated function.

questions.q: Given `std::unique_ptr<Instrument> p = std::make_unique<Future>(...)`, what happens when you call `p->price()` if price() is declared virtual in Instrument?
options: It always calls Instrument::price(), regardless of the actual object type
It fails to compile because Instrument is abstract
It dispatches at runtime to Future's override of price()
It calls both Instrument::price() and Future::price()
questions.explain: Virtual functions enable dynamic dispatch: calling through a base pointer or reference resolves to the actual derived type's implementation at runtime.

questions.q: What goes wrong if a base class's destructor is NOT declared virtual, and you delete a derived object through a base-class pointer?
options: Nothing — destructors are always virtual automatically
The program fails to compile
Only the base class's destructor runs, potentially leaking resources the derived class owns
Only the derived class's destructor runs
questions.explain: Without a virtual destructor, delete through a base pointer calls only the base destructor — the derived class's cleanup code never runs.

questions.q: In `class Future : public Instrument`, what does the `public` keyword specify?
options: That all of Future's own members are public
The type of inheritance — public inheritance preserves the base class's access levels for external code
That Instrument's private members become accessible to Future
That Future can be converted to any other type
questions.explain: Public inheritance means Instrument's public interface remains public when accessed through a Future object — the normal, most common form of inheritance for an is-a relationship.
